body.en: A formula that is true for every assignment of truth values is a *tautology* (valid), e.g. p ∨ ¬p. One that is false for every assignment is a contradiction (unsatisfiable), e.g. p ∧ ¬p. One that is true for some and false for others is a contingency. A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes it true, so every tautology and every contingency is satisfiable.

say.en: A formula that is true for every assignment of truth values is a tautology valid, e.g. p ∨ ¬p. One that is false for every assignment is a contradiction unsatisfiable, e.g. p ∧ ¬p. One that is true for some and false for others is a contingency. A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes it true, so every tautology and every contingency is satisfiable. Tautology: all 1 second in the result column.
Contradiction: all 0 seconds.
Contingency: some 1 second, some 0 seconds.
Satisfiable: at least one 1.

body.en: To prove an equivalence without a truth table, rewrite one side step by step, naming the law used at every step. Typical moves: replace → by ¬p ∨ q (implication law), push ¬ inside brackets (De Morgan), remove double negations (involution), factor out a common term (distributive) and remove p ∧ ¬p or p ∨ ¬p (complement). A formula is a *tautology* if it simplifies to 1.

say.en: Show that (p ∧ q) gives p is a tautology using laws.
(p ∧ q) gives p = ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ p implication law.
= (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ p De Morgan.
= (¬p ∨ p) ∨ ¬q (commutative and associative).
= 1 ∨ ¬q equals 1 (complement, then p ∨ 1 equals 1).
So the answer is It simplifies to 1, so it is a tautology.
